metadata.title: An Ogilvy Lens on SignalBrief — Duc
metadata.ogilvy_note: Food for thought — not a grade. Ogilvy is one lens among several, running alongside the course rubric. The maker decides.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN — ClaudeComposerAsk. Liam asks the Ogilvy question.
beats.narration_text: Duc's SignalBrief pitch. A weekly decision brief for AI infrastructure founders — collects public developer signals from HackerNews, GitHub, and dev.to, ranks them, recommends what to build, monitor, or ignore. What would David Ogilvy ask about it?

props.command: I just watched Duc's SignalBrief pitch — a weekly decision brief for AI infrastructure founders, pulling developer signals from HackerNews, GitHub, and dev.to, ranking them, and recommending actions with source links. What do David Ogilvy's principles say about how this pitch frames the work? Not a score, not a verdict. Just the questions a great ad man would ask.

beats.role_note: Show Slide 1 (problem), then rebuild as Brutalist. The headline is strong Ogilvy copy.
beats.narration_text: Let's start with the opening claim. The loudest post keeps winning the roadmap. That is a strong Ogilvy headline — concrete, felt, already true before the deck opens. The three-column breakdown underneath it earns its place: three hours weekly of scanning, signal gets buried, roadmaps drift. Not padded. This slide knows what it is doing.

beats.act: LENS 1 — The IP Taxonomy: Why Is It on Slide 4?
beats.role_note: Show Slide 4 (evidence taxonomy), rebuild. The four-tier framework is the real moat — Ogilvy: lead with the main message.
beats.narration_text: Slide 4 is where the real IP lives. Discussed — developer debates. Explained — practitioner posts. Adopted — repo adoption. Verified — weak data labeled. AI explains the trend; trust comes from the sources. This is not a feature list. It is a trust architecture. Ogilvy would call this the main message. It is sitting on slide 4. The question worth sitting with: what is it doing there instead of slide 2?

beats.act: LENS 2 — The Distinction: Monitors vs. Deciders
beats.role_note: Show Slide 7 (competition), rebuild. The competitive frame is precise and earns its place.
beats.narration_text: The competition slide earns its keep. Monitors send alerts. SignalBrief recommends action. Feedly feeds, not decisions. F5Bot keywords, not ranking. Brand24 brand alerts, not roadmap action. None of them decide. Ogilvy: specifics in a comparison always outperform generalities. This one lands. The one sentence at the top of the slide is the whole pitch.

beats.act: LENS 3 — Name Clarity: One Name, All the Way Through
beats.role_note: No slide — pure observation. 'Signal Proof' in the room vs 'SignalBrief' on the deck.
beats.narration_text: One thing to reconcile before the next pitch. In the room you introduce it as Signal Proof. The deck says SignalBrief. They are not the same name. Ogilvy was ruthless about this: a name that cannot survive a five-minute presentation will not survive a market. This is not a branding lecture. It is a practical note. Pick one name. Own it completely. Never waver.

beats.act: LENS 4 — The Buried Hero: 3 Hours to 10 Minutes
beats.role_note: Show Slide 9 (POC stats), rebuild. The strongest value claim is only in the narration, never on a slide.
beats.narration_text: The proof-of-concept slide has strong numbers — one hundred eighty records, batch run in twenty-four seconds, three priority signals produced. That is engineering proof. But in the narration you say the product turns a three-hour scan into ten minutes. That is the hero. That is the value proposition in one sentence. It does not appear on any slide. Put it on the deck, at the top, where it earns its keep.

beats.act: LENS 5 — The Ask: Give It a Job Description
beats.role_note: Show Slide 10 (ask), rebuild. Five design partners is the right ask — but what do they commit to?
beats.narration_text: The ask slide is clean. Help SignalBrief reach paid pilot. Five design partners, access to founder communities. That is the right stage to be at. But a design partner needs a job description. What does a good one commit to — a weekly read, a feedback session, a willingness to test a price? The ask is strong enough to carry one more sentence. Give it one.

beats.role_note: Not a verdict: four questions for the next draft.
beats.narration_text: Not a verdict — a lens set. Four questions for the next draft. One: which name are you building — Signal Proof or SignalBrief? Two: the evidence taxonomy is your moat — why is it sitting on slide 4 instead of slide 2? Three: three hours to ten minutes is your hero number — where is it on the slides? Four: what does a design partner actually commit to? Give the ask a job description. These are Ogilvy's questions. The pitch decides which ones matter.
